summary: Psalm 60 begins with a national crisis: God is addressed as the one who has rejected, shaken, and wounded the people, and the speaker asks for restoration. The poem then recalls God’s claim over Israel’s territories and neighboring peoples, before returning to the question of who will lead them against Edom. It ends by rejecting merely human help and trusting that victory must come through God.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how Israel’s prayer book can hold military defeat, divine anger, national identity, and renewed trust in one poem. It also shows how a heading can connect a psalm with remembered conflict while the prayer itself remains the main guide to its meaning.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with David, but Psalms as a book is a many-voiced anthology, and the exact force of such headings is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Psalms contains poems and collections from different periods; assigning one date to the whole book, or to every Davidic heading, would be misleading.
context.setting: Book II of Psalms, among prayers that include distress, royal hope, national memory, and trust. This chapter’s heading places it in a setting of conflict with Aram and Edom.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a historical heading, communal lament, divine speech, questions, and a closing statement of trust.

outline.heading: Heading and plea after rejection
outline.note: The heading names a tune, a teaching poem, David, and battles; the prayer opens by saying God has rejected and broken the people and asks him to restore them.

outline.heading: The land and people shaken
outline.note: The speaker describes the land as trembling and torn, and the people as made to drink staggering wine.

outline.heading: A banner and a plea for rescue
outline.note: God has given a banner to those who fear him, and the speaker asks him to save his beloved ones with his right hand.

outline.heading: God’s claim over lands and peoples
outline.note: God speaks from his sanctuary, claiming places within Israel and speaking triumphantly over Moab, Edom, and Philistia.

outline.heading: The unresolved way to Edom
outline.note: The speaker asks who will bring him into the strong city and faces the painful claim that God has not gone out with the armies.

outline.heading: Help beyond human strength
outline.note: The psalm asks God for help against the adversary and ends in confidence that through God the people will act valiantly.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. To the tune of “The Lily of the Covenant.” A teaching poem by David, when he fought with Aram Naharaim and with Aram Zobah, and Joab returned, and killed twelve thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt. God, you have rejected us. You have broken us down. You have been angry. Restore us, again.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives both the heading’s battle setting and the opening lament: the crisis is interpreted as rejection by God, not only as military trouble.

keyVerses.text: So that your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and answer us.
keyVerses.why: The psalm’s complaint turns into a direct request for rescue, naming the people as God’s beloved even while they feel rejected.

keyVerses.text: Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine. Ephraim also is the defense of my head. Judah is my scepter.
keyVerses.why: This line anchors the divine speech by presenting Israel’s regions and tribes as belonging to God and serving his rule.

keyVerses.text: Through God we will do valiantly, for it is he who will tread down our adversaries.
keyVerses.why: The final verse gathers the psalm’s hope: the people may act courageously, but their victory is attributed to God.

questions.question: Why does the psalm start with so much historical detail?
questions.answer: Verse 1 includes a heading that names a musical direction, a tune, a teaching poem, David, Aram, Joab, Edom, and the Valley of Salt. Such headings are ancient features of the Psalter, but readers differ on whether they function as authorship, association, collection, dedication, or remembered setting. Follow the poem’s own movement from defeat to appeal to confidence.

questions.question: What is a “teaching poem”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the heading of verse 1. It signals that the psalm is not only an emotional cry but also a poem meant to instruct its hearers in how to understand crisis before God. The heading does not explain the technical term further, so it is best not to overdefine it.

questions.question: Does the psalm say the people’s suffering comes from God?
questions.answer: Yes, the speaker directly addresses God: “you have rejected us,” “You have broken us down,” and “You have been angry.” The chapter presents the crisis as experienced in relation to God, not merely as enemy action. It does not explain the reason for the anger in this chapter.

questions.question: Is the trembling land an actual earthquake or an image for national collapse?
questions.answer: Verse 2 says, “You have made the land tremble. You have torn it.” The line can evoke an earthquake while also picturing the community’s collapse; the psalm does not identify a particular earthquake. In the chapter, the point is clear enough: the crisis feels like the land itself has been fractured and needs God to mend it.

questions.question: What does the “wine that makes us stagger” mean?
questions.answer: Verse 3 pictures the people as forced to drink something that leaves them unstable and reeling. The line belongs to the psalm’s description of hard things God has shown the people. It is poetic language for disorientation under judgment or disaster, not an instruction about wine.

questions.question: What is the “banner” in verse 4 doing?
questions.answer: The banner is given to those who fear God and is displayed “because of the truth.” In a battle-shaped psalm, a banner suggests a rallying sign, but the verse ties it to reverence and truth rather than mere morale. The chapter does not give enough detail to reconstruct an exact ritual or military practice.

questions.question: Why does God name places like Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah?
questions.answer: In verses 6-7, God speaks as owner and ruler over named lands and tribes. The list grounds the prayer’s hope in God’s claim over the people and their territory. The chapter’s emphasis is not geography for its own sake but divine authority over the places named.

questions.question: Why are Moab, Edom, and Philistia described so sharply?
questions.answer: Verse 8 uses images of dominance: Moab as a wash basin, a sandal thrown on Edom, and triumph shouted over Philistia. These are ancient victory images within a battle psalm, not a direct modern policy statement. The poem depicts God’s rule over hostile neighbors from Israel’s perspective in crisis.

questions.question: How can the psalm say God rejected them and still end with confidence?
questions.answer: The psalm never denies the rejection language; verse 10 repeats it. But it also asks God for help and concludes that “Through God we will do valiantly.” The movement is not from certainty that nothing is wrong, but from crisis to renewed dependence on God rather than on human help alone.

glossary.def: A preserved performance marker in verse 4. Its exact force is uncertain, so it is best read as a signal from the psalm’s musical or liturgical setting rather than translated as a normal word.
A rallying sign in verse 4, given by God to those who fear him and displayed because of the truth.
The holy place named in verse 6 as the source from which God speaks.
The opponent named in verse 11. The psalm asks God for help against this enemy because human help is vain.
